entries.title: Russell Brand and the media that made him
entries.summary: A rape conviction for the British comedian and actor leads to a reckoning for the media that kept him in the spotlight.
entries.content:
The Listening Post

Russell Brand and the media that made him

A rape conviction for the British comedian and actor leads to a reckoning for the media that kept him in the spotlight.

The conviction of comedian and actor Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault is a moment of reckoning for Britain’s entertainment industry. Some of the country’s most influential media institutions gave him the platforms, credibility and audiences that made him such a prominent public figure, and continued to do so as more and more allegations of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour surfaced.

Contributors:

Dorothy Byrne – Former head of news and current affairs, Channel 4

Caroline Frost – Entertainment journalist

Dalia Gebrial – Lecturer, King’s College London and author of Decolonising the University

Ellie Tomsett – Film and media lecturer, Birmingham University

On our radar:

Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s last major independent newspaper, has been forced to shut down after years of pressure from the authorities.

Meenakshi Ravi reports on how the outlet went toe-to-toe with the Kremlin.

Australia’s gambling industry: the ads, the money, the lobby

From slot machines to betting apps, gambling is a big part of Australian culture. Advertisers know it is something people often do with friends, and they have tapped into that trend. Australians are bombarded with slick marketing that promotes betting with mates.

Elettra Scrivo reports on one of the world’s most entrenched gambling industries, the advertising that props it up and the lobby that protects it.

Featuring:

Alex Russell – Research Fellow, Experimental Gambling Research Lab

Kate Seselja – Founder, The Hope Project Australia and co-chair, Gambling Harm Lived Experience Experts

Steve Cannane – Reporter, ABC Australia Four Corners

entries.title: ‘My arms are empty’: Tragedy strikes Gaza family after baby dies from cold
entries.summary: A nine-month-old baby has died from hypothermia inside his family’s displacement tent in Gaza, as winter returns.
entries.content:
A nine-month-old baby has died from hypothermia inside his family’s displacement tent in Gaza, as winter returns.

Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For Susan Arqiq, the hardest part of the day comes at night, when the noise around her fades and she is left alone with the absence of her nine-month-old son, Kinan. She is still struggling to understand how the cold took his life.

Susan, 26, had put him to sleep beside her on Wednesday night, as she had done countless times before, at their camp in Khan Younis. When she woke in the early hours of the morning to change his diaper, she found Kinan’s face blue, his hands stiff and his body cold.

Her arms, which had held him through countless nights, are now empty.

“My son was pressed against the tent’s tarpaulin. The bedding was still damp,” she told Al Jazeera.

“I switched on my phone’s flashlight and found that his face was completely blue, his hands were stiff, and his body was like ice. My heart nearly stopped from fear. I immediately woke my husband. I was screaming, ‘Kinan, Kinan!’ I could not understand what was wrong with him.”

Her husband did not speak. He picked up the baby and, accompanied by men from the camp, rushed him to hospital.

Women from neighbouring tents, woken by the cries, gathered around Susan. They tried to reassure her that her baby would be all right, but the news from the hospital confirmed her fears.

Kinan died on Thursday, November 12, after a severe drop in his body temperature, according to medical sources. His death was the first cold-related fatality recorded in Gaza during the current winter season.

Susan and her husband, Ahmed Arqiq, 33, have been in shock since the tragic death of their son. Ahmed says Kinan had no known health problems before that night.

“At the emergency department, they told me, ‘May God compensate you. The child has died, and the cause is the severe drop in temperature,’” Ahmed says. “I was shocked… My heart is broken, and even now I cannot believe it.”

A tent cannot keep out the cold

Israel’s war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, has seen at least 73,600 Palestinians killed and large parts of the occupied Palestinian territory reduced to rubble. Due to the destruction of their homes or Israeli military occupation, around 1.4 million people are living in tents or makeshift displacement camps.

Israel’s siege on Gaza has prevented mobile homes, tarpaulins, and other essential materials from entering the territory.

The Arqiq family are one of many living in a worn-out displacement tent in the al-Mawasi camp near Khan Younis in southern Gaza as winter approaches. The shelter offers little protection from the cold or the rain, which flooded camps across Gaza during a storm last week.

Ahmed has been unable to find work since the war, and they struggle to afford even the basic necessities of life.

“I have struggled to obtain adequate shelter, blankets, clothing and food for my children. My life is all about suffering,” he said. “Look at my tent. We live in poor conditions. During the last winter storm, we were flooded with water.”

Ahmed said the family had not received a proper tent or tarpaulin to protect them from the winter weather before Kinan’s death. After Kinan died, they received the waterproof sheet, but it was too late to protect him.

Kinan was the youngest of three children, and his brothers, Rami, three, and Ali, two, were deeply attached to him. They continue to ask about their younger brother, unable to understand why he is no longer with them.

“They always ask where he has gone. Whenever they see his belongings, they try to look for him. It is unbelievable,” Ahmed said.

A winter that brings new fears

Kinan’s death has renewed fears among displaced families in Gaza as winter sets in. Last week, heavy rain and flooding battered displacement camps across Gaza, damaging tents and leaving families exposed to cold and wet conditions. At least four children died in the floods.

Babies are particularly vulnerable to hypothermia as their bodies are less able to regulate temperature, especially when exposed to cold for prolonged periods.

At least 11 people are believed to have died due to the cold in Gaza last winter.

Hadeel al-Midana, 27, lives in a displacement tent west of Gaza City with her three children: Hamza and his two older brothers, Mahmoud, seven, and Nour al-Din, five. Her husband, Ibrahim, has been out of work since the war.

She said Kinan’s death has deepened fears she carries each night when she tries to keep her own youngest son, one-month-old Hamza, warm.

“I am always on edge. I cannot leave him,” she told Al Jazeera.

The family struggles to keep the children warm with limited clothing and blankets.

“I swear, he doesn’t have a blanket of his own. I wrap him in the blankets that I use myself,” Hadeel says, referring to Hamza.

The family has received second-hand clothes from neighbours. They were also provided with four blankets at the camp, but Hadeel said the cold inside their tent remains difficult to endure.

“Even the adults cannot bear it. How much worse is it for the little children?” she asked.

She wakes up several times during the night to check on Hamza. Two nights ago, she found his hands and feet were as cold as ice. Terrified, she covered him with a thicker blanket.

She says she needs more blankets for her baby and a small bed to lift him off the ground.

“I need blankets for him, and perhaps a bed that would raise him a little above the ground. I am afraid of the insects, too,” she said.

“The tent is not fit for a child’s life, or even an adult’s life. We live in constant fear, and there is nothing we can do to face it. I hope we get through this winter safely.”

entries.title: Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb
entries.summary: Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces retreat from the Red Sea coast, threatening global maritime security.
entries.content:
Houthi fighters are edging closer to the temporary capital following a sudden withdrawal of government-aligned forces from the Bab al-Mandeb area.

Forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government face a potentially catastrophic situation, as Houthi forces advance on the southern city of Aden and other strategic areas.

Yemeni government forces said on Sunday they had withdrawn from Dhubab airport and territory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, southwest of Yemen, to defend Aden, the de facto seat of the government.

Retired Lebanese Brigadier-General Hassan Jouni, a military and strategic expert, said fighting is now focused on control over a mountainous triangle of territory in southern Yemen, which could decide the outcome of the war.

This area links Aden to Taiz, another city held by the government but encircled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – and Bab al-Mandeb, a maritime chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

“This triangle is the strategic centre of gravity for the war in Yemen as a whole,” Jouni told Al Jazeera.

On Sunday, government-aligned forces were withdrawn from Dhubab, which was recaptured from the Houthis in September, to avoid an imminent siege in the coastal strip by the Houthis and to help defend Aden, analysts say.

Houthi advances in this southwestern region now threaten to completely cut off the government’s coastal supply routes, Jouni said.

The Yemen war began when the Houthis, a Zaidi Shia group close to Iran, captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south to Aden. Saudi Arabia launched an Arab coalition military campaign to aid the government in March 2015, launching thousands of air strikes against Houthi forces.

Following a relatively peaceful few years, fighting re-erupted in July when government forces’ jets bombed Sanaa international airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital.

A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha. Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.

Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat from Dhubab, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.

“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.

But Jouni believes the situation faced by government forces is grim, with the Houthis reaching Tor al-Baha, just 80km (50 miles) from Aden.

“The Houthi forces have reached this line, meaning that they are indeed in the defensive line area of the city of Aden. We do not say they have approached Aden, but the defence of the city of Aden begins in this area,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The basic combat direction now is in the vicinity of the besieged city of Taiz. On the other hand, of course, the Houthis will focus their attention now on approaching Aden and controlling the first defensive zone.”

Strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab gave a less optimistic assessment of the situation than the one presented by the government.

“What happened is a retreat or a withdrawal with the same meaning, and not a redeployment, because the withdrawal left a vast vacuum filled by the Houthis,” al-Dahab stated.

Regional escalation

The government’s “Operation Yemen Dawn” has responded to the situation with a dramatic increase in strikes on Houthi positions, including 900 targeting operations within 24 hours.

The Houthis have responded with ballistic missiles and drone attacks towards Mecca, Riyadh, and the Eastern province in Saudi Arabia. They have announced they will continue operations under a principle of “siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation”.

Al-Dahab said this strategy is directed at Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s key international ally, and not at authorities in Aden.

With their recent gains on the coast along Bab al-Mandeb, which has become increasingly significant to global maritime trade since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran, the Houthis have significant geopolitical leverage.

“They now directly and completely control the western Yemeni coastal sector and part of the maritime extension towards Aden,” al-Dahab warned.

“The matter translates the Houthis’ gains in Bab al-Mandeb in large part to the benefit of Iran.”

entries.title: Jailed Pakistan ex-PM Imran Khan writes to judges, seeks vital medical care
entries.summary: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party founder says court orders on his care were ignored and he ‘may not return alive’.
entries.content:
The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party founder says court orders on his care were ignored and he ‘may not return alive’.

Islamabad, Pakistan – Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan’s top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, in an open letter released by his lawyer.

Lawyer Salman Safdar posted the letter on X on Monday, describing it as a “humanitarian plea for medical treatment”. It is Khan’s first such letter since he fell ill earlier this year.

Safdar said Khan gave him instructions and notes during a three-hour meeting at Central Jail Rawalpindi, also known as Adiala Jail, on November 11, and that he prepared the letter solely on that basis.

Khan, 74, has been in jail since August 2023, following convictions that his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), says are politically motivated.

In the letter, he said he had been held in solitary confinement “for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025, when he and Bushra Bibi were sentenced to 17 years in one of several cases against them.

He said he had lost 85 percent of the vision in his right eye and that doctors had told him he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

Khan wrote that he had “never once sought relief on medical grounds, nor used illness as a tactic”.

“I fought on the merits, with confidence, and I still do,” he said. “I do not ask Your Lordships for any favour.”

On August 18, the Supreme Court ordered that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and examined by a medical board. “That order has not been implemented,” he wrote.

Instead, he was taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) and returned to jail within hours.

Khan was taken to hospital again late on November 10 for an eye injection. PIMS said he was “clinically stable”, while Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said he was receiving the required care.

Khan also raised concerns about Bushra Bibi, whom he married in 2018. He said she suffered a retinal detachment in April and underwent “complicated eye surgery in secrecy”.

Without another operation, he said, “she may lose her sight permanently”.

Her lawyers filed an application at the Islamabad High Court on Monday seeking her complete medical record and immediate transfer to a specialised hospital.

Two of Khan’s sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were released from a Lahore jail on November 12 after nearly two months in detention. Aleema Khan, a third sister, remains in jail, according to PTI.

The government said it detained the sisters over a possible threat to law and order in advance of PTI’s Islamabad march planned for September 27, which did not go ahead.

Sayed Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader, said ex-PM Khan had been left with no other option but to seek further legal intervention.

“He’s been left with no choice but to write this open letter because, over three years of imprisonment and solitary confinement, he has seen that justice has only been seen in small flashes and then gone away,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera.

Bukhari said the letter did not mean Khan was giving up.

“He is asking for no favours. He is asking for no deal. He is asking for justice and the legal system of Pakistan to work,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera. “All it shows is a man humbly asking for justice and humane medical treatment.”

Bukhari said the party wanted the courts to press the government to act.

“We want the courts to hear his proceedings adequately … rather than adjourning and postponing them,” he said. “And we want the courts to apply enough pressure on the government that real medical treatment should be provided so that there is no loss of life, no loss of vision.”

Mehmal Sarfraz, a Lahore-based political analyst, said the letter reflected Khan’s concern about his wife’s health.

“He is very worried about his wife’s deteriorating health and is looking for relief for her,” Sarfraz told Al Jazeera.

Another Lahore-based political analyst, Habib Akram, said he did not see the letter as a plea for mercy.

“If he were asking for mercy, he would not have needed to write this letter. He has written to the courts, not to anyone else,” Akram told Al Jazeera. “And what is he asking for? He is asking for his rights, which he has cited from the jail manual.”

Akram, however, was sceptical that the letter would change Khan’s circumstances.

“What is being done to Imran Khan has lost its legal grounds. The Islamabad High Court has an order that he can meet visitors on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The Supreme Court has also ruled. Neither was followed, but a third order was suddenly complied with,” he said.

“This is no longer a legal issue. I don’t think the Supreme Court’s order will be implemented because of this letter.”

entries.title: Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Kenya’s elusive black leopard
entries.summary: Maasai photographer Latei Moses searches Kenya for the rare wild cat, telling his own story through his lens.
entries.content:
Witness

Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Kenya’s elusive black leopard

Maasai photographer Latei Moses searches Kenya for the rare wild cat, telling his own story through his lens.

Maasai photographer Latei Moses is on a journey across northern Kenya to fulfil a lifelong ambition: to photograph the elusive black leopard, known locally as Giza. Believed to inhabit the remote region of Laikipia, the wild cat has long been the subject of local stories.

Latei’s search takes him across difficult terrain, as he faces repeated setbacks and exhaustion. But his journey is about more than wildlife. The Maasai are among the most photographed communities in the world, often depicted through the eyes of outsiders. As a Maasai photographer, Latei is reclaiming the power of the camera, documenting his people on his terms. But can his persistence help him find Giza?

Beyond the Horizon: Searching for Giza is a documentary film by Mohtadi Ali Ahmad, Mohamad Ali Ahmad and Christelle Saade.

entries.title: Russian attacks kill three in Ukraine, EU accuses Moscow of prolonging war
entries.summary: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Russian President Vladimir Putin is making maximalist demands.
entries.content:
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Russian President Vladimir Putin is making maximalist demands.

Russian attacks have killed at least three people in Ukraine, as the European Union accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, killing a man on a moped, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.

Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk region’s military administration.

Elsewhere, a 59-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack in the village of Bilenke in the southern region of Zaporizhia, said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the region’s military administration.

Monday’s attacks come as EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of making maximalist demands in a bid to extend the conflict.

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

“In 2021, Russia’s demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going,” Kallas said in a post on X.

“A ceasefire must come first. It must be the basis to start the talks about anything else. With EU Foreign Ministers, we will discuss our own demands on Moscow to reply to the maximum demands that Russia is presenting.”

Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks in the Belgorod region of southwest Russia killed one person on Monday, local authorities said.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that it had intercepted 1,336 drones during overnight attacks by Ukraine.

Kyiv received $1.88bn from the European Commission on Monday to buy drones, ammunition and air ⁠defence systems. The money is part of a larger $99bn loan approved in February. Separately, the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine, about $8.7bn.

“Thank you to [the] EU Commission and EU Council for approving the largest-ever single payment to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility, amounting to nearly €8 billion [$8.7bn],” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

“I thank President Von Der leyen for her personal efforts to expedite the preparation of this payment, given Ukraine’s growing budgetary needs ahead of winter and intensified Russian attacks on our energy, heating, water supply, and other critical infrastructure.”

The EU is currently pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half-year conflict.

The bloc on Monday imposed more sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 50 banks and financial institutions. Several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil, and petroleum products were also sanctioned.

Dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.

Last week, two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials were held in the United Arab Emirates.

The discussions were mediated by the US and led to an agreement on a prisoner exchange. However, they failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war.
